chunks: "For an ideal inductor the impedance is j omega L . At DC, omega is zero, so the impedance is zero: it's a short circuit.
As frequency goes to infinity, the magnitude omega L goes to infinity, so it's an open circuit.
If I plot magnitude against frequency on linear axes, it's a straight line through the origin with slope 2 pi L .
On log–log axes, which is how you'd normally draw it, it's a straight line going up at 20 decibels per decade: ten times the frequency, ten times the impedance.
The phase is a constant plus 90 degrees. Then I'd add what a real inductor does, because the ideal plot is wrong at both ends.
At low frequency it doesn't go to zero; it flattens out at the DC resistance of the winding, maybe tens of milliohms.
And at high frequency the capacitance between turns resonates with the inductance.
The impedance peaks at the self-resonant frequency, and above that it actually falls, because the part behaves like a capacitor.
So a 10 microhenries power inductor might peak in the tens of megahertz and be useless as an inductor above that.
So in practice: short at DC, rising impedance through the useful band, and you design to stay well below SRF."
